body:
Fixes #5995.

## What

`json_value::destroy_container()` and `destroy_walk()` (both `noexcept`, reached from `data::~data()`) held the containers they tear down in default-constructed `basic_json` stand-ins. Each one constructs a `CustomBaseClass` that belongs to no value: one per destroyed container, four per level in `destroy_walk()`. A base class whose default constructor allocates (a long `std::string` member, say) made destruction allocate again, and terminate when that allocation failed, which is what #5762 set out to prevent (#5135).

The stand-ins now are `data` (`m_type` and `m_value`, no base class). `struct data` is forward-declared before `union json_value`, and `take`, `has_no_children`, `all_children_leaves`, `walk_child`, `pop_walk_child`, `free_container`, `destroy_bounded` and `destroy_walk` take `data&`; real children are passed as `child.m_data` / `child.second.m_data`. The algorithm itself is unchanged. `take()` already moved only `m_data`, so `m_parent` under `JSON_DIAGNOSTICS` is handled as before.

## Tests

`unit-custom-base-class.cpp`, "destroying a value does not construct the custom base class": a counting base class checks that destroying a scalar, a small array/object document and a value nested 1000 levels deep (alternating arrays and objects, so `destroy_walk()` walks both) constructs no base object and destroys exactly one per value. Without the fix: 1 construction and one extra destruction per case.

The reproducer from the issue (allocating base class under a fail-at-k `operator new`) now ends with `no throw at k=12: done`, with and without `JSON_DIAGNOSTICS=1`; before, it terminated.

Not addressed here (mentioned in the issue as related): the unconditional `noexcept` on `basic_json(basic_json&&)` with a base class whose move constructor can throw.

## Public API

No breaking changes. Only private members of `json_value` change their parameter types.

comments.body:
### Performance check

**No performance impact.** Destruction is hot (every DOM parse and copy ends in it), so I checked it on both compilers.

- **Generated code** (clang, arm64): `json_value::destroy_bounded()`, the recursive part that destroys every normal document, is **instruction-for-instruction identical**. Only its signature changes (`data&` instead of `basic_json&`). With the default empty base class, `basic_json` and `data` have the same layout, so the stand-ins compile to the same code. Only `destroy_walk()` differs, in register allocation and one store. It runs only for nesting deeper than `recursion_depth_limit()`.
- **Instruction counts** (each case includes destroying the result):

| case | clang/arm64 PR/base | GCC/x86-64 (callgrind, exact) PR/base |
|---|---:|---:|
| parse twitter | 1.0011 | 1.00000 |
| parse citm_catalog | 1.0011 | 1.00000 |
| copy twitter | 1.0003 | 1.00000 |
| copy citm_catalog | 1.0033 | 1.00000 |
| copy canada | 0.9997 | 1.00000 |

  GCC differs by at most 10 instructions per document. The clang rows are within the noise band, as expected for identical code. With a non-empty `CustomBaseClass` the PR saves the base-class construction per destroyed container, which is the point of #5995.

<details><summary>Method</summary>

- PR head vs. its base (merge base), both compiled into one binary (namespaces renamed per copy) with the same workload: DOM parse (string, stream, callback), copy/destroy, `==`/`<`, iteration, `dump()`, msgpack/UBJSON/BJData read and write, `json_document` parse/`dump()`/`==`/`get<std::int64_t>()` on twitter, citm_catalog, canada and small_signed_ints.
- **Generated code**: both variants disassembled (Apple clang 21, `-O3`, arm64), names and addresses masked, compared function by function.
- **Instruction counts**: Apple M1 Max, instructions retired per repetition (minimum of 3 runs, setup subtracted). Rows whose machine code is identical vary by about ±0.4 %, which is the noise floor. Where a hot path changes, also GCC 13.3 `-O3` on x86-64 under callgrind, which gives exact counts (built with `-falign-functions=64 -falign-loops=64` unless a row says otherwise).
</details>

---

review_comments.body: This would allow someone to write `swap(json_value& a, json_value& b)` and intercept this call.  I don't see a reason to support this.  Using `std::swap()` would make sure that this is exactly as expected.

Right: nothing should be able to customize the swap of the internal `json_value`, and the unqualified call would pick up such an overload through ADL. Fixed in 110d38635a: it is now `std::swap(cur.m_value, *this)`. This resolved to `std::swap` before as well, so behaviour does not change.

*(Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.)*
